items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we are given the graph of the function [MATH: y=f(x)] defined on the interval [MATH: [-2,2]] as shown below. How can we calculate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-2}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/11e34fd87d7c70132a2719d0983e1f84]

Content:
First, we notice that the graph consists of two parts: the line segment for [MATH: x \in [-2,0]] and the line segment for [MATH: x \in [0,2].] Therefore, using the additive property of the definite integral, we can write the integral as follows:
[MATH: \int_{-2}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = \underbrace{\int_{-2}^{0} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{A_1} + \underbrace{\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{A_2}]

Content:
Now, we use the fact that the area of the region between the graph and the [MATH: x]-axis can be represented using definite integrals. We divide the region between our curve and the [MATH: x]-axis as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4e667270304346790dc6d0a5fe41544c]

Content:
The first integral represents the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis, where [MATH: x \in [-2,0].] The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

Content:
[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2)(a + b)h; = (1)/(2)(1 + 2) ⋅ 2; = 3.]

Content:
The second integral represents the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis, where [MATH: x \in [0,2].] The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

Content:
[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2)ab; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 2 ⋅ 2; = 2.]

Content:
So, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{− 2}^{2}f(x)dx|= A_{1} + A_{2}; = 3 + 2; = 5.]

Consider the graph of the function [MATH: y=f(x),] shown below. It consists of three line segments. Find the value of
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x.]

[IMG: /graphics/9945bb9e16c42b2c41ed53b402e96364]

sections.normalized_html:
The graph consists of [MATH: 3] parts: the line segment for [MATH: x \in [0,2],] the line segment for [MATH: x \in [2,3],] and the line segment for [MATH: x \in [3,4].] Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:

[MATH: \int_{0}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = \underbrace{\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{A_1} + \underbrace{\int_{2}^{3} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{A_2} + \underbrace{\int_{3}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{-A_3}]

The [MATH: 1]st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis, where [MATH: x \in [0,2].] The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2)(a + b)h; = (1)/(2)(2 + 3) ⋅ 2; = 5.]

The [MATH: 2]nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis, where [MATH: x \in [2,3].] The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2)bh; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ 3; = (3)/(2).]

The [MATH: 3]rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis, where [MATH: x \in [3,4].] The corresponding region is also a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

[MATH: A_{3}|= (1)/(2)bh; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ 1; = (1)/(2).]

Since the region lies below the [MATH: x]-axis, we have

[MATH: \int_{3}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = -A_3 = -\dfrac{1}{2}.]

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{4}f(x)dx|= A_{1} + A_{2} − A_{3}; = 5 + (3)/(2) − (1)/(2); = 6.]

The [MATH: 2]nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis, where [MATH: x \in [-2,0].] The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

The [MATH: 3]rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis, where [MATH: x \in [0,2].] The corresponding region is a quarter-circle, so we find the area using the formula
